text.tspan: 05 · src/ code map — what is built, what is deliberately empty

Conclusion: the governed decision path is real, dependency-free, exhaustively tested code; the model invocation and the three lane services are NOT implemented, and nothing in the repository fakes them.
api/client.ts + api/types.generated.ts — types are GENERATED from the
contracts by scripts/generate-api-types.mjs and drift-checked in CI.
state/asyncState.ts + AsyncBoundary.tsx — the five required view states.
Screens are still PlaceholderScreen: the shell is real, the beats are not.
Creates the six containers in the local Cosmos emulator, which Terraform
cannot reach. The duplication with infrastructure/cosmos.tf is deliberate
and guarded: scripts/policy-cosmos-containers-match.sh fails the build if
the two ever disagree about a name or a partition key.
src/router-service · the only path to a model
Correlation/CorrelationIdMiddleware.cs — one id, end to end
Security/ApprovalsAuthorization.cs — Proposer and Approver app roles,
caller identity read from the token oid claim, never from the body (ADR-011).
Persistence/ApprovalStore.cs — IN-MEMORY today; Cosmos is T-014a.
Every refusal is audited too: "someone tried to approve their own
proposal and was stopped" is the record an auditor comes looking for.
DOMAIN ASSEMBLIES — the rules live here, never in an endpoint
Handlers translate HTTP and nothing else. A rule reachable only through a controller is a rule that can only be tested through a socket.
No ASP.NET, no Azure SDK, no clock.
That is what makes it exhaustively
The strongest statement it can make
not a receipt. Whatever acts must
so the repository carries the recipe
NOT IMPLEMENTED — and drawn here so the gap is visible rather than assumed
Awaiting the Azure subscription window. ADR-007: when a dependency is unreachable the system says which one and refuses — it never substitutes a recorded result.
The persistence suite runs against a real Cosmos engine in Docker and fails with instructions when it is absent, rather than skipping green.
Governed chokepoint / deterministic code the exchange depends on.
Human-in-the-loop. A person, holding a distinct identity, decides.
Synthetic data and the tests that prove the rest.
NOT implemented. README only, or an explicit NotInvoked.
How to read this repository in the right order
Start at src/Fcmr.Router.Decisions. It has no dependencies, it holds every routing rule, and it is the only assembly the demo's central claim actually
rests on — governance decides, the application does not.
Then src/Fcmr.Approvals.Domain, which holds the human gate and, deliberately, no ability to act on it.
The services above them are thin on purpose: if you find a rule inside an endpoint, that is a defect, not a shortcut.
Everything in the dashed red band is absent, not hidden. The demo can currently prove its governance and its privacy; it cannot yet prove an end-to-end
model call, and it does not pretend to.
